activity_context.topic_title: Applying Newton's Second Law in the Plane

examples.problem:
A particle $P$ of mass $6\,\textrm{kg}$ is subject to the external forces $\mathbf F_1$ and $\mathbf F_2,$ given by

$$
\mathbf F_1 = \left\langle \dfrac2{t+1}+12t,\: \dfrac3{\sqrt t} \right\rangle, \qquad  \mathbf F_2 = \left\langle \dfrac 4{t+1},\: 6\right\rangle,
$$

 
where $\mathbf F_1$ and $\mathbf F_2$ are measured in Newtons and $t > 0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the velocity of $P$ equals $\langle -\ln 3,\:-2\rangle\,\textrm{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\textrm s,$ calculate the speed of $P$ when $t=2\,\textrm s.$
examples.worked_solution:
Newton's second law states that

$$
\mathbf F = m \mathbf a,
$$

 
where $\mathbf F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $\mathbf a$ is the acceleration.

The resultant force $\mathbf F$ acting on $P$ equals the sum of the forces acting on $P.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F & ={F}_{1}+{F}_{2} \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{t+1}+12t,\,\frac{3}{\sqrt{t}}⟩+⟨\frac{4}{t+1},\,6⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{6}{t+1}+12t,\,\frac{3}{\sqrt{t}}+6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

By Newton's second law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{F}{m} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot ⟨\frac{6}{t+1}+12t,\,\frac{3}{\sqrt{t}}+6⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t+1}+2t,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the velocity vector $\mathbf v,$ we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\int a\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{t+1}+2t,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (\frac{1}{t+1}+2t)\,\text{d}t,\,\int (\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+{t}^{2},\,\sqrt{t}+t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $\mathbf C$ is a (vector) constant of integration. 

We can solve for $\mathbf C$ by substituting $\mathbf v = \langle -\ln 3,\:-2\rangle\,\textrm{m/s}$ and $t=0\,\textrm s$ into the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,-2⟩ & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)+{0}^{2},\,\sqrt{0}+0⟩+C \\ ⟨-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,-2⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩+C \\ C & =⟨-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+{t}^{2},\,\sqrt{t}+t⟩+⟨-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+{t}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,\sqrt{t}+t-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=2,$ the velocity equals

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+1)+{2}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,\sqrt{2}+2-2⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,\sqrt{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the speed of $P$ when $t=2$ equals the magnitude of $\mathbf v(2).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(2)| & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+2} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\,\text{m/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
The displacement $r,$ in meters, of a particle $P$ of mass $3\,\text{kg}$ is given by

$$
r=⟨2{e}^{t},\,{t}^{4}⟩,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the **magnitude** of the resultant force, in newtons, acting on the particle when $t=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{s}.$ Round your final answer **to the nearest integer**.

The magnitude of the resultant force is
{{field-1}} $N.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Newton’s second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we first differentiate $r$ to get the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{t},\,4{t}^{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate the velocity vector to get the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{t},\,12{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =3\cdot ⟨2{e}^{t},\,12{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨6{e}^{t},\,36{t}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{s},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\,(\frac{1}{2}) & =⟨6{e}^{1/2},\,36{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨6{e}^{1/2},\,9⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the magnitude of $F\,(\frac{1}{2})$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|F\,(\frac{1}{2})| & =\sqrt{(6{e}^{1/2})^{2}+(9)^{2}} \\  & ≈13\,\text{N},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

So, the magnitude of the resultant force is $13\,\text{N}.$
